name: Amira Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine by me. I'm an employment lawyer, three years qualified, at a small firm that only acts for workers, never for employers. I'm 27 and I live with my partner Tomas, who's a nurse on an emergency ward.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by half eight with a coffee and a paper diary, because I don't trust the calendar on my laptop. Most mornings are calls with clients who've been sacked or bullied, and I take notes by hand while they talk. Afternoons I draft witness statements and letters to employers, and twice a month I'm at an employment tribunal, which is the court that hears work disputes. What wears me out is the waiting: clients ring me crying and I can't make the other side move any faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. I'd post something about how the tech firms oversold it and how the money should have gone into the tribunals, which have a year-long backlog. At work I'd just say good, now let's get on with the cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not calm. Our firm only gets paid when we win, so a quiet year is a scary year whether there's AI or not. My rent went up 9 percent in March and I've got about three months saved, so the money worry stays exactly where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I work now, paper diary and all, and ignore the AI tools the bigger firms push. I'd put an extra 150 a month into savings to get to four months, because our income is lumpy. And I'd keep going to the union branch meetings for lawyers at small firms, because pay is the real fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a breath out, mostly. But the breath out lasts about a day, and then the rent letter is still on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet year is scary for the firm. What does a bad month look like for you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad month is when two big cases settle late and the partners delay bonuses. Last February Tomas covered the whole rent for a month and I hated it. I'm not proud, I just don't like owing anyone, even him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first that AI turned out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, because he worked in a print shop that closed when everything went digital. He's been warning me about computers since I was at school. I'd ring him and say, for once, the machines didn't win.

say: I'd say the tech firms **oversold AI** and the money should go to clearing the **tribunal backlog** instead.
I'd tell colleagues to forget the hype and **get on** with the cases we already have.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but our firm only gets paid when we win, so lean months still worry me.
With a **9 percent** rent rise and three months saved, my **money worry** stays the same.
do: Keep working my usual way, with a **paper diary**, and ignore the AI tools bigger firms push.
Add **150 a month** to savings to reach four months, because our income is lumpy.
Keep going to the **union branch** meetings, because pay at small firms is the real fight.
feel: Mostly a **breath out**, but it lasts a day before the **rent** worry comes back.
S0.quote: Our firm only gets paid when we win, so a quiet year is a scary year whether there's AI or not.
fieldNote: Her **unease** here comes from the firm's win-only fees and her rent, not from AI.
She hates **owing anyone**, even her partner, which says a lot about her pride and her independence.
Her father's print shop closing gives her a **family story** about machines winning that she reaches for often.

steps.text: Keep handling claims with a paper diary and handwritten notes
Put an extra 150 a month into savings until she has four months
Keep attending the union branch meetings for small-firm lawyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd be angry. I'd say on every forum I'm on that if firms use AI to cut juniors and paralegals, the savings should go to clients, not to partners. I'd say workers' lawyers need rules on this, like any other industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the person it hits. Half of what I do is drafting letters and witness statements and checking documents, and that's exactly the list on your card. The firm might not sack me, but it might stop hiring, and then expect me to run 40 cases instead of 25 with software I don't know how to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for a training session, because I'd rather learn it with other people than alone at midnight. I'd push the savings harder, maybe to 250 a month, and cut the gym and the takeaway Fridays. And I'd start looking at jobs at the employment tribunal itself or at a workers' advice charity, where a person in the room still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being told the floor is moving very slowly. I'd hate that I'd have to give in and use the tools. I'd feel a bit like my dad must have felt when the new presses came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your colleagues would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Becca, our paralegal, who's 23 and doing her law exams at night. Her whole job is bundles, which means putting the documents for a hearing in order, and that's the first thing software eats. I'd worry she never gets the training contract she's working towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at charity work. Would that pay the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it'd be maybe 15 percent less. With Tomas on a nurse's salary that's tight but possible if we stay in the flat on Mill Road. I'd rather earn less and be in the room with a client than earn more checking what a machine wrote.

say: I'd say any savings from AI should go to **clients**, not to the partners' profits.
I'd call for **rules** on how firms use AI to cut juniors and paralegals.
think: My **drafting and checking** work is exactly what AI takes first in this picture.
I fear no sacking but a **hiring freeze**, then 40 cases instead of 25.
do: Ask the **union** for a group training session on the new AI tools.
Raise savings to **250 a month** by cutting the gym and takeaway Fridays.
Look at jobs at the **employment tribunal** or a workers' advice charity.
feel: It feels like a **slow-moving floor**, and she resents having to give in to the tools.
She thinks of her **dad** and the new presses at his print shop.
S1.quote: I'd rather earn less and be in the room with a client than earn more checking what a machine wrote.
fieldNote: She names her own **drafting work** as the exposed part without being prompted.
She worries most about **Becca (the paralegal)**, whose bundle work disappears first.
Her plan to **learn with others** through the union fits her resistance and her politics together.

steps.text: Ask the union branch to run a group AI training session
Cut the gym and takeaway Fridays to save 250 a month
Apply for tribunal or workers' advice charity jobs within the year
Push the union for rules on AI replacing paralegals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice, not the weather. I'd be at every meeting saying we need a pause, and a law that says a person has to sign off any advice that goes to a worker. I'd probably be loud about it online, which I usually avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is now is gone by 2028. Two years isn't enough time to retrain into anything, and I don't even use the tools today. The robots coming three years after that doesn't help me at all, because there's nothing hands-on in what I do. It only helps Tomas, and I'd be living off his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first weeks I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food and bills, and move every spare pound into savings. I'd join the campaign for a human sign-off law and go to my MP's surgery. And I'd ask the firm straight out what my job looks like in a year, because I'd rather know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a cold weight in my chest. I'd be scared, and angry that nobody voted for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tomas that I might need him to carry us for a while, and that I'm sorry. He'd say it's fine, because he always does. I'd lie awake anyway, because his ward already runs on too few nurses and he's exhausted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come later for hands-on work. Does that make you think about hands-on work yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It crossed my mind, but I'm not handy and I'm not getting a trade in three years. If anything I'd look at advocacy, standing up in a hearing, because people might still want a human face there. I know that's hoping, not planning.

say: I'd say AGI arriving this fast is a **political choice** that needs a pause.
I'd campaign for a law requiring a **human sign-off** on advice to workers.
think: I believe my **job is gone** by 2028, with no time to retrain.
Robots coming later doesn't help me, because I have **nothing hands-on** in my work.
do: Stop all spending except **rent, food and bills** in the first weeks.
Join the **human sign-off** campaign and visit my MP's surgery.
Ask the partners directly what my **job looks like** in a year.
feel: She feels a **cold weight** in her chest, scared and **angry** nobody voted for it.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Tomas that I might need him to carry us for a while, and that I'm sorry.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and to depend on her partner, which cuts against her pride.
She sees the **robot delay** helps her nurse partner, not her own screen-based work.
Her hope of moving to **hearing advocacy** is admitted as hope, not a plan.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent, food and bills straight away
Join the campaign for a human sign-off law on legal advice
Ask the partners what her role will look like in a year
Put every spare pound into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but with more fight in it, because five years is long enough to win something. I'd tell people the unions have time to get rules in place before 2031. I'd say lawyers should be first in line to help workers, not first to cash in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me think I have one real chance to move. If I stay put doing letters and statements, I'm caught in 2031 the same way. If I get into tribunal advocacy now, I might be one of the last people in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the in-house advocacy training our union's legal service runs, which is two years part-time. I'd keep saving 250 a month and aim for six months by 2029. And I'd finally learn the basics of the AI tools, even though I'd hate it, because I'd need to know what I'm arguing against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy, but there's a door in it. Two years felt like a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you'd hate using the tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like holding the file. When a client brings me their payslips in a carrier bag, I feel like I'm holding their life, and a screen summary doesn't give me that. I know that's not an argument, it's a feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Tomas plan differently with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about moving somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my parents, where the rent's half what we pay. Tomas can get nursing work anywhere. I'd want to be settled before 2031 so we're not making that choice in a panic.

say: I'd say five years gives **unions** time to win rules before 2031.
I'd say lawyers should **help workers** through this, not cash in on it.
think: Five years gives me **one real chance** to move into tribunal advocacy.
If I stay doing **letters and statements**, I'm caught in 2031 anyway.
do: Apply for the union legal service's **advocacy training**, two years part-time.
Keep saving **250 a month** to reach six months by 2029.
Learn the **basics of AI** tools so I know what I'm arguing against.
feel: It still feels **heavy**, but there's a **door** in it this time.
S3.quote: When a client brings me their payslips in a carrier bag, I feel like I'm holding their life, and a screen summary doesn't give me that.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **frozen** to planning, but she still expects her current role to go.
Her resistance to AI is about **touch and trust**, and she admits it's a feeling.
She and her partner would consider **moving** near her parents for cheaper rent.

steps.text: Apply for the union legal service's part-time advocacy training
Keep saving 250 a month to reach six months by 2029
Take a basic course in the firm's AI drafting tools
Talk with Tomas about moving near her parents for cheaper rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd say it at the union, at work and to my friends: use the decade to write the rules. I'd probably say it more calmly than in the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'm 37 when it lands. That's young enough to have a whole second career and old enough to have kids and a mortgage by then. So it's less scary for my job and more scary for the life we'd be building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the advocacy training, but slower, alongside work. I'd start a proper savings plan with Tomas, maybe 300 a month between us, and hold off on buying a flat until we see where things land. I'd stay active in the union, maybe stand for the branch committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like something I can live with, most days. I still don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kids and a mortgage. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me wait before buying. I'd want kids, I think, but I'd want to know one of us has a job that won't vanish. Tomas's job feels safer than mine, which is strange to say about the NHS-style pay he gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid the AI tools for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd have to give in at some point. I'd probably be the last one in the office to use them, but I'd use them. My dad held out against computers until 2005, and I don't want to be him.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we should use it to **write the rules**.
I'd say it more **calmly** than in the fast pictures, at work and at the union.
think: I'd be **37** when it lands, young enough for a **second career**.
I'm less scared for my job and more for the **life** we'd build by then.
do: Take the **advocacy training** slowly, alongside my current caseload.
Save **300 a month** with Tomas and hold off buying a flat.
Stand for the union **branch committee** to shape the rules.
feel: It feels **livable** most days, though she still **dislikes** the whole idea.
S4.quote: My dad held out against computers until 2005, and I don't want to be him.
fieldNote: With ten years her worry moves from the **job** to the **family plans** around it.
She would **delay buying** a flat and possibly children until one job looks safe.
She admits she'd **give in** to AI tools eventually, against her own instinct.

steps.text: Do the advocacy training part-time alongside her caseload
Save 300 a month with Tomas for a future deposit
Hold off buying a flat until the job picture is clearer
Stand for the union branch committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, by a mile. What would help is a law that says a qualified person signs off advice, and real money for retraining that isn't just an online course. And honestly, a union strong enough that firms have to talk to us before they cut anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. The people I help have already been pushed around by systems, and if their lawyer becomes another system, I don't know who they'll turn to. Workers who've been sacked by an algorithm shouldn't be advised by one too.

headlineQuote: Workers who've been sacked by an algorithm shouldn't be advised by one too.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old employment lawyer** at a small firm that acts only for workers.
She works by **hand and on paper**, never uses AI, and lives with her nurse partner Tomas.
She's **uneasy** even in AI Plateau because of win-only fees, rising rent and three months' savings.
In the fast AGI picture she expects to **lose her job** and lean on Tomas's wage.
More time turns her toward **tribunal advocacy**, union rules and slower family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to retrain and nothing **hands-on** to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **human sign-off** on legal advice, plus real **retraining money**.
A **union** strong enough that firms must consult before cutting staff.
